description: Flat 8 m square of large pale granite flagstones in a running bond -- the temple courtyard surface, as one quad and one seamless PBR texture set.

image.prompt:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: Flat square of large rectangular pale granite paving slabs seen as a single unbroken surface, EVERY slab the same size at 1 metre by 2 metres so exactly four slabs span the 8 metre square across and eight courses run down it, laid flat in straight parallel courses with the joints of each course offset by half a slab from the course before, tight fine joints, no small slabs and no mixed sizes anywhere, slabs varying slightly in tone, edge to edge stone only, no kerb and no border Materials: Seamlessly tiling pale grey and warm buff granite with a fine speckled crystal grain, slab faces worn smooth and softly polished along the walked lines with a rougher flame-finish grain elsewhere, tonal drift slab to slab from near white to mid grey, dark grime and thin moss lines in the joints, pale wax and candle spotting, faint bleached rings where water pools and dries, a few chipped slab corners and one hairline-cracked slab; the slab coursing must wrap on all four edges so a run of tiles gives unbroken continuous joint lines.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

name: Temple Granite Flagstone Tile
nameTh: พื้นหินแกรนิตลานวัด
notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The entire surface reads out of the texture; the slab joints are a normal and AO groove rather than modelled geometry. This is a member of the kit's ground-surface tile set: every tile in that set is 8 x 8 m, sits at y=0, uses pivot base-center and snaps on the kit's 8 m grid, so it butts flush against any other ground tile and against the asphalt road tiles, and the raised Concrete Sidewalk Strip (2.0 m wide, 0.15 m tall) sits alongside as a separate object. It exists to fill a specific hole in this kit: the monumental set already has a Chedi, an Ubosot, a Prang, a Reclining Buddha Hall, a Khmer Stone Sanctuary, a Chinese Shrine and a Mosque, and there is no courtyard surface to stand any of them on -- a wat compound is a broad expanse of large pale stone slabs, and putting one of those buildings on asphalt or on grey block paving is what makes a temple scene read wrong. The slabs are laid in a running bond with offset joints, so this tile is only TWO-way rotationally symmetric: it drops in at 0 or 180 degrees, and a 90 degree rotation turns the coursing across the run, which is visible and is sometimes what a builder wants at a change of level or direction. The course pitch must divide 8 m evenly and wrap on all four edges, or every tile boundary shows a half slab -- that is the first thing to check on the generated texture. One risk specific to this tile: a pale flat stone surface can land close to the reference plate's grey backdrop and confuse a silhouette gate, so the generated plate needs real slab-to-slab tonal variation rather than one even tone. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. No destruction groups: a ground tile is static level geometry, not a breakable.
